core_classification.analysis: The words name a conventional avowal but are not themselves used to avow love: the speaker invokes the formula while declaring it unsayable under an imagined dissolution of the separate “I” and “you.” T receives slight support from the formula’s retained semantic content, while O captures its dominant metalinguistic and repudiated-hypothetical force.
core_classification.ambiguity: The quoted formula can be analysed either as a merely mentioned expression or as an imagined avowal whose presupposed speaker–addressee structure is being rejected; neither reading makes it an actual love declaration.

other_diagnosis.tpe_failure: T/P/E do not adequately represent the token’s principal force: it metalinguistically exhibits a familiar love formula in order to deny that such an utterance can occur within the described state of undifferentiated oneness.
other_diagnosis.core_not_context: This is a property of the embedded token’s use—quotation under “Nor can I say”—rather than merely surrounding emotional or narrative context.

utterance_status.description: A quoted, contemplated love utterance embedded under “Nor can I say”; it is invoked as an utterance rendered impossible by the imagined loss of distinct speaker and addressee.

contextual_interpretation: The passage contrasts speech, which requires separate persons, with a mystical or erotic consummation in which “I” and “you” have been transcended. “I love you” is therefore cited as the paradigmatic speech of separate subjects and rejected as inapplicable to the silent, unified state being described. There is no evidence of a commitment or affect-driven verbal discharge.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “Nor can I say ‘I love you,’ when I have ceased to be, and you have ceased to be”
evidence.supports: The love formula is quoted beneath an explicit denial of the speaker’s ability to utter it, supporting hypothetical/metalinguistic rather than assertoric force.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “Speech travels between the separate parts. But in the perfect One there is perfect silence of bliss.”
evidence.supports: The passage treats the formula as structurally dependent on separate interlocutors and contrasts it with silence, explaining why T/P/E alone miss the token’s dominant use.

evidence.quotation_or_description: “there was no I and you ... we are both caught up and transcended into a new oneness”
evidence.supports: The rejected utterance serves a philosophical account of merged identity rather than functioning as a direct declaration, undertaking, or reflexive discharge.

evidence.quotation_or_description: The occurrence is identified as appearing in Chapter XXVII of D. H. Lawrence’s Women in Love.
evidence.supports: Establishes the bibliographic and structural location of the passage without adding interpretive facts beyond the supplied text.

ontology_assessment.diagnosis: O accommodates the case, but the compact ontology is strained because the highlighted words are meaningfully cited as an impossible utterance rather than used with ordinary truth-conditional, performative, or expressive force.
ontology_assessment.candidate_recurrent_dimension: Metalinguistic or exhibited mention of a love formula whose applicability is explicitly denied.
